The conflict between the concepts of collective and private ownership that has led to litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property is in reality a debate over whether individuals should act as titleholders or merely as caretakers with respect to their property.

The conflict between the concepts of collective and private ownership that has led to litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property cannot be resolved until the rights of native Canadians have been comprehensively defined in Canadian law.

The conflict between the concepts of collective and private ownership that has led to litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property illustrates the need to expand the concept of private property to include cases of joint ownership by a collection of individuals.

questions.prompt: According to the concept of private property as presented in the passage, which one of the following most completely describes the meaning of the term "property owner"?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The term in question is "property owner", but we're not looking for just *any* definition of property ownership. Specifically, we're looking for the definition of "property owner" "*according to the concept of private property."* Rather than searching "property" or "owner," which are both found all over this passage, it would be smart to start by searching for the first keyword: "private."

The first three hits this search returns are all in the first lines of P2 so that is the natural place to start researching. When reseraching a Semi-Defined Target, starting with the first mentions of the keyword is usually the right move. The first sentence tells us that under the concept of private property Canadian courts usually base their decisions on, "all forms of property are capable of being owned by individuals or by groups functioning legally as individuals." Dumbed down, this seems to mean that all property can be owned by a single person or a group that is treated like a single person under the law.

The question is asking which answer "most completely describes the meaning of the term." That first line doesn't feel like a very complete picture of property ownership, so it makes sense to keep reading. Line 2 tells us "the system is based on a philosophy that encourages the right of owners to use their property as they see fit without outside interference." Dumbed down, if you own it, you can use it however you want and nobody can tell you otherwise.

Line 3 starts with the pivot word "But" which tells us that what follows is going to be diffferent and therefore probably NOT part of the definition we're looking for. This means our research is done and we can make a prediction.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something like "a person or a group can own something and use it how they want to without outside interference."

choices.text: one who possesses a bill of sale to substantiate his or her claims to property ownership
choices.explanation:
The first two sentences of the 2nd paragraph define *property owner*, in the private property concept, as "an individual or a group functioning legally as an individual that can use the property as they see fit without outside interference".

There's nothing in those two lines about possessing proof of prior possession.This idea does come up in P3: "Museums, which are likely to possess bills of sale or proof of prior possession to substantiate their claims of ownership..." But this is not part of the *definition* of property ownership that we're given. It's just cited as a *reason* courts have historically sided with museums in ownership disputes.

choices.text: one who possesses proof of prior possession to substantiate his or her claims to property ownership
choices.explanation:
The first two sentences of the 2nd paragraph define *property owner*, in the private property concept, as "an individual or a group functioning legally as an individual that can use the property as they see fit without outside interference".

There's nothing in those two lines about possessing proof of prior possession. Like for answer A, this idea does come up in P3: "Museums, which are likely to possess bills of sale or proof of prior possession to substantiate their claims of ownership..." But this is not part of the *definition* of property ownership that we're given. It's just cited as a *reason* courts have historically sided with museums in ownership disputes.

choices.text: one who is allowed to make use of his or her property in whatever manner he or she wishes
choices.explanation:
The first two sentences of the 2nd paragraph define *property owner*, in the private property concept, as "an individual or a group functioning legally as an individual that can use the property as they see fit without outside interference".

"Make use in whatever manner he or she wishes" is a pretty good match for "use as they see fit without outside interference".

choices.text: one who is allowed to transfer ownership rights to his or her children as heirs
choices.explanation:
The first two sentences of the 2nd paragraph define *property owner*, in the private property concept, as "an individual or a group functioning legally as an individual that can use the property as they see fit without outside interference".

There's nothing in those two lines about being allowed to transfer ownership rights. This does come up at the end of P2 when the author speaks on the different definition of communal property: "nor does it pass to their heirs when they die." It's reasonable to infer from that contrast indicator "nor" that the private property definition of ownership DOES imply the transfer of ownership to heirs. Nonetheless, this is not the most *complete* definition, and that's what the question stem is asking for.

choices.text: one who is allowed to exercise property rights because of his or her membership in a community
choices.explanation: This is offering a definition that sounds more like communal property ownership, not ownership in the private property concept.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the possibility of courts increasingly assigning ownership rights to native communities is best described as which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's final sentence is where we find her attitude about the forthcoming future of court decisions:

*But as their awareness of the* *****inappropriateness***** *of applying the private property concept to all cultural groups grows, Canadian courts* *****will***** *gradually recognize that native Canadians can* *****clearly***** *claim ownership as prescribed by the notion of collective property.*

The author sounds firmly convinced that native Canadians *should* have their property rights recognized under the notion of collective property, and convinced that Canadian courts will eventually agree with her.

choices.text: certain that it will never be realized and concerned that it should
choices.explanation: The author says that "Canadian courts ****will**** recognize that native Canadians can claim ownership via collective property".

choices.text: concerned that it will never be realized but hopeful that it will
choices.explanation: The author says that "Canadian courts ****will**** recognize that native Canadians can claim ownership via collective property".

choices.text: uncertain whether it will be realized but hopeful that it will
choices.explanation:
The author says that "Canadian courts ****will**** gradually recognize that native Canadians can claim ownership via collective property".

Here the author predicts that the recognition will occur, rather than expressing uncertainty about whether it will occur. The word 'will' is a future prediction in this context, not a standalone conditional rule.

choices.text: uncertain whether it will be realized but confident that it should
choices.explanation:
The author says that "Canadian courts ****will**** gradually recognize that native Canadians can claim ownership via collective property".

Here the author predicts that the recognition will occur, rather than expressing uncertainty about whether it will occur. The word 'will' is a future prediction in this context, not a standalone conditional rule.

choices.text: convinced that it will be realized and pleased that it will
choices.explanation:
The author says that "Canadian courts ****will**** gradually recognize that native Canadians can claim ownership via collective property". So the author is convinced it will be realized.

The author also said that Canadian courts will grow increasingly aware of the ****inappropriateness**** of the current status quo (applying private property) rights. She also says that native Canadians ****clearly**** can claim ownership and their claims ****should**** be honored.

So, yes, she is fully on board with this emerging reality.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the first paragraph of the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: The existing problem is that courts generally apply private-property standards, while native communities make collective-ownership claims and rarely possess the documents required by the private-property concept. Recent litigation calls museums' ownership into question. explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: The first paragraph provides the background on the Old, on the Problem, and ends with the pivot into the New: *recent litigation* looks like it might go a New way and be somewhat of a Solution.

choices.text: identify some of the specific types of property at issue in litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property from museums
choices.explanation:
Although the first paragraph does have a hyphenated aside that says "artifacts ranging from domestic implements to ceremonial costumes", that was not at all a focus of the paragraph.

This answer doesn't speak to the big Framework chunks: the background of the Old Problem, and the teaser thesis in the final sentence of the New Solution.

choices.text: describe the role of the concept of property ownership in litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property from museums
choices.explanation: This answer summarizes the role of the 2nd paragraph, not the 1st.

choices.text: summarize the difficulties that have been experienced in attempting to develop a comprehensive definition of the rights of native Canadians under the law
choices.tag: Too Narrow / Word Bait: comprehensive definition
choices.explanation:
Just like (A), this answer matches up with one sentence, but not even the main clause of that sentence, an aside or a dependent clause.

This is just trying to get people to pick an answer that sounds like the very first sentence.

We're not told any story about all the difficulties that have transpired as they attempt to develop a comprehensive definition of rights.

The passage immediately leaves that intro sentence's wide angle and zooms in on "rights regarding movable cultural property". And the passage is about the difficulties Native Canadians have experienced in trying to assert their property rights, using a notion of collective property.

It's not about the difficulties Canadian legislators have experienced while trying to formulated clear laws, as this answer describes.

choices.text: provide the context within which litigation by native Canadians to regain control of their movable cultural property is occurring
choices.explanation:
This might not be how we pre-phrased it, but we can match this up.

The final sentence of the paragraph is about the *recent litigation* that will dominate the rest of the passage. And the rest of the first paragraph does provide the contextual backdrop leading up to this recent litigation:

- it's apparently part of a broader period of flux within the native Canadian legal space, where the legal rights of native Canadians are not yet defined. It's within this context of, "our legal system is still figuring out how to handle native Canadian rights" that we get this passage, which is saying, "One big epiphany the legal system has had in regards to native Canadians is that we'll have to recognize the concept of communal property employed by these communities, or else we'll hardly ever recognize their property rights!"

choices.text: discuss the difficulty of deciding legal cases that rest on a clash between two cultures’ differing definitions of a legal concept
choices.explanation: This answer is speaking to the difficulty of deciding cases that rest on a clash between private property and communal property, but this distinction isn't even brought up until the 2nd paragraph.

questions.prompt: Given the information in the passage, Canadian courts hearing a dispute over movable cultural property between a museum and a group of native Canadians will be increasingly unlikely to treat which one of the following as a compelling reason for deciding the case in the museum's favor?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The keywords "increasingly unlikely" map to the final sentence of the passage, where we are told how Canadian courts are changing, going forward:

*But as their awareness of X grows, Canadian courts **will gradually** recognize that native Canadians can clearly claim ownership as prescribed by the notion of collective property (even though they cannot demonstrate ownership as prescribed by the notion of private property).*

So, currently/previously, a court would decide in favor of the museum, because "native Canadians rarely possess the legal documents that the concept of private property requires to demonstrate ownership, whereas museum are likely to possess bills of sale or proof of prior possession to substantiate their claims of ownership".

In short, courts have been siding with museums because museums have "the receipts" for the cultural property in question. Native Canadians don't, because the whole tribe owns this property collectively. No individual member possesses a deed of ownership.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: If courts are going to gradually realize that native Canadians can claim ownership through the notion of collective property, then they will be unlikely to treat "museum has receipts, natives don't" as a reason for deciding in favor of the museum.

choices.text: The museum is able to produce evidence that the property did not originate in the native community.
choices.explanation:
This is close to what we're looking for, but not quite right (so probably not an accident that it's in slot A).

We're looking for, "the museum is able to produce written evidence of ownership for that property, whereas the native community is not".

This isn't saying that the museum has evidence saying THEY own the property. It's saying that the museum has evidence saying that the natives DON'T own the property.

Proving a positive vs. proving a negative

To make this answer an even worse match, it's also not saying "evidence that the natives don't own the property"; it's saying "evidence that the property didn't **originate** in their community", which is a separate concept altogether that the passage didn't discuss.

choices.text: The museum cannot produce written documentation of its claims to ownership of the property.
choices.explanation: We were looking for, "the museum CAN produce written documentation of its claims to ownership, whereas the native community cannot".

choices.text: The group of native Canadians produces evidence that the property originated in their community.
choices.explanation:
This would have never been a reason for siding with the museum. This is a reason to side with the native community.

We're looking for the old reason why courts sided with museums: "they had receipts, whereas the natives did not".

choices.text: The group of native Canadians cannot produce written documentation of their claims to ownership of the property.
choices.explanation: The final paragraph predicts growing recognition of collective ownership despite the absence of the documents private-property rules require. On that account, native Canadians' lack of written documentation will become less compelling as a reason to decide for museums. This is an increasing unlikelihood, not a claim that documentation will cease to matter in every case.

choices.text: The group of native Canadians do not belong to a tribe that employs a legal system that has adopted the concept of private property.
choices.explanation:
We're looking for the old reason why courts sided with museums: "they had receipts, whereas the natives did not".

The courts were never siding with museums because of what type of legal system the natives had.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the concepts of collective and private ownership differ in each of the following ways EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
If we ask our brain, "What are a couple differences between collective vs. private ownership?" and have retained a couple distinctions, then we should head into the answers.

If our question to our brain comes up blank, we should go back to the 2nd paragraph to scan for some reminders.

**Private** - something is owned by an individual, or group of people functioning as an individual (like a corporation). the individual owner can do whatever they want with the property without outside interference.
**Collective** - something is owned by the entire community equally. everyone has a say in how a commonly owned resource is used. you are limited in what you can do with your ownership of property by "the collective interests of the community".

**Private** - you own a title, a document showing your proof of ownership. Your property is passed down to heirs when you die..
**Collective** - you have no written proof of ownership. Your property does not pass down through inheritance (kids are owners simply in virtue of being community members)

choices.text: The collective concept allows groups of individuals to own property; the private concept does not.
choices.explanation:
The first sentence of the 2nd paragraph contradicts this. The private concept does allow for groups to own property.

We're told that under the private property concept, "all forms of property are capable of being owned by individuals **or by groups** functioning legally as individuals."

choices.text: The collective concept requires consideration of community interests; the private concept does not.
choices.explanation:
We were told that under the private concept, owners have a right to use their property as they see fit without outside interference.

We were told under the collective concept, "use of resources is determined by the collective interests of the community".

choices.text: The collective concept assigns ownership on the basis of membership in a community; the private concept does not.
choices.explanation: Under collective ownership, membership in the community itself assigns an ownership right. Under the private-property concept, an individual or a group functioning legally as an individual can own property, with documents used to demonstrate that ownership. Membership alone and proof of an individual title are distinct grounds; documents demonstrate a claim rather than creating every private ownership right by definition.

choices.text: The private concept allows owners to function as titleholders to their property; the collective concept does not.
choices.explanation:
In the beginning of the 3rd paragraph, it implies that private ownership is based on legal documents that demonstrate that *you* are the titleholder to this piece of property.

At the end of the 2nd, "collective ownership casts an individual in the role of the guardian or caretaker of property, **rather than as a titleholder**".

choices.text: The private concept permits individuals to sell property; the collective concept does not.
choices.explanation:
The beginning of the 2nd paragraph tells us that private ownership allows you to use your property in any way you see fit, including selling it, without outside interference.

The end of the 2nd tells us that in a collective ownership system, "individual members **cannot sell** this right".

questions.prompt: The passage most supports which one of the following statements about the tribal legal systems mentioned in the second paragraph of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
If we re-read the available text in the 2nd paragraph about *tribal legal systems*, it just says that *some tribes now recognize the notion of private property in their legal systems, but they have traditionally employed a concept of collective ownership*.

There might be a trap answer speculating the causal backstory of why tribal legal systems now contain some recognition of private property, but we don't know why they now do.

The correct answer is probably going to take a detail we hear about *collective ownership* elsewhere in the passage and apply it to the traditional workings of these tribal legal systems.

choices.text: All tribes whose legal system employs the concept of collective property have engaged in litigation over control of movable cultural property.
choices.explanation:
We can't derive that 100% of tribes who use the concept of collective property have litigated to regain control over movable cultural property.

The passage just said that 100% of tribes who have litigated to regain control over movable cultural property have used the concept of collective property.

choices.text: Only tribes that have engaged in litigation over control of movable property have a legal system that employs the concept of collective property.
choices.explanation:
This is literally the same sentence as (A), which would tell you that they're both wrong.

"Only" indicates the necessary condition, so just like (A), this would be diagrammed as

*if employs concept → engaged in litigation*
*of collective property over control of*
*movable property*

We were told the Reversed Logic version of this.

choices.text: All tribes that have engaged in litigation over control of movable cultural property have a legal system that employs the concept of collective property.
choices.explanation:
We are told that "in all cases in which they've made legal claim to movable property they have done so by invoking this concept of collective ownership".

So that would look like

*if engaged in litigation invoked concept*
*over control of movable → of collective*
*cultural property ownership*

This answer is just taking it one inferential step further:

"if a tribal system invoked the concept of collective ownership, then they employ the concept of collective property".

That's basically a self-justifying truth, so we're fine with that extra little language move.

choices.text: All tribes whose legal system recognizes the concept of private property can expect to succeed in litigation over control of movable cultural property.
choices.tag: Too Strong: all / Out of Scope: can expect to win
choices.explanation:
The only thing we can say about the "some tribes" that now recognize private property is that they have traditionally ****employed**** a concept of collective ownership and in all cases in which they've ****made**** legal claim to movable cultural property they've invoked the concept of collective ownership.

Notice that all we know is past tense stuff. This answer is saying we can derive a forward-looking prediction that they can expect to win all their court cases!

choices.text: Only those tribes whose legal system recognizes the concept of private property can expect to succeed in litigation over control of movable cultural property.
choices.explanation:
Did the author ever say about these tribes in the 2nd paragraph that "if they don't recognize the concept of private property, they can never expect to succeed in litigation over control of movable cultural property"?

No, that's way stronger than anything we can find in the 2nd paragraph.

passages.title: Embryo Polarity
passages.text:
The first thing any embryo must do before it can develop into an organism is establish early polarity—that is, it must set up a way to distinguish its top from its bottom and its back from its front. The mechanisms that establish the earliest spatial configurations in an embryo are far less similar across life forms than those relied on for later development, as in the formation of limbs or a nervous system: for example, the signals that the developing fruit fly uses to know its front end from its back end turn out to be radically different from those that the nematode, a type of worm, relies on, and both appear to be quite different from the polarity signals in the development of humans and other mammals.

In the fruit fly, polarity is established by signals inscribed in the yolklike cytoplasm of the egg before fertilization, so that when the sperm contributes its genetic material, everything is already set to go. Given all the positional information that must be distributed throughout the cell, it takes a fruit fly a week to make an egg, but once that well-appointed egg is fertilized, it is transformed from a single cell into a crawling larva in a day. By contrast, in the embryonic development of certain nematodes, the point where the sperm enters the egg appears to provide crucial positional information. Once that information is present, little bundles of proteins called p-granules, initially distributed uniformly throughout the cytoplasm, begin to congregate at one end of the yolk; when the fertilized egg divides, one of the resulting cells gets all the p-granules. The presence or absence of these granules in cells appears to help determine whether their subsequent divisions will lead to the formation of the worm’s front or back half. A similar sperm-driven mechanism is also thought to establish body orientation in some comparatively simple vertebrates such as frogs, though apparently not in more complex vertebrates such as mammals. Research indicates that in human and other mammalian embryos, polarity develops much later, as many stages of cell division occur with no apparent asymmetries among cells. Yet how polarity is established in mammals is currently a tempting mystery to researchers.

Once an embryo establishes polarity, it relies on sets of essential genes that are remarkably similar among all life forms for elaboration of its parts. There is an astonishing conservation of mechanism in this process: the genes that help make eyes in flies are similar to the genes that make eyes in mice or humans. So a seeming paradox arises: when embryos of different species are at the one-or few-cell stage and still appear almost identical, the mechanisms of development they use are vastly different; yet when they start growing brains or extremities and become identifiable as distinct species, the developmental mechanisms they use are remarkably similar.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

How embryos across different species establish polarity (body orientation), and how this phase differs from later development

**Framework**

Old / New (There is also a strong "Highlight Noteworthy" element as the passage spotlights a paradox, but the main structure is an Old/New contrast between early vs. later mechanisms.)

**Main Point**

The earliest step in embryonic development—establishing polarity (front/back, top/bottom)—uses very different mechanisms across species, but for later developmental stages, like forming limbs and organs, animals rely on remarkably similar genetic processes. (The Most Valuable Sentence is in the last paragraph: "So a seeming paradox arises: when embryos of different species are at the one-or few-cell stage and still appear almost identical, the mechanisms of development they use are vastly different; yet when they start growing brains or extremities and become identifiable as distinct species, the developmental mechanisms they use are remarkably similar.")

**P1: Introducing Embryonic Polarity and Its Diversity**

All embryos must first establish their basic body orientation (polarity), but the ways in which different organisms create this early spatial framework vary a lot—the signals flies use, for example, are very different from those used by nematodes or mammals.

**P2: How Different Species Establish Polarity**

The paragraph details how specific animals get polarity started: fruit flies prepare the "instructions" in the egg before fertilization; nematodes use the site of sperm entry as a guide, moving certain proteins to help create body orientation; some simple vertebrates use a sperm-driven cue, but mammals don't seem to. In humans and other mammals, polarity happens much later and the process remains mysterious.

**P3: Paradox—Similarity in Later Development**

Once body orientation is set up, all animals rely on a surprisingly similar set of genes to develop complex structures like eyes and limbs. This creates a paradox where embryos use very different strategies early on, but later use almost identical ones to elaborate their body plans.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Species differ more in the mechanisms that determine the spatial orientation in an embryo than they do in their overall genetic makeup.
Embryos determine their front from their back and top from bottom by different methods, depending on whether the organism is simple or more complex.

While very similar genes help determine the later embryonic development of all organisms, the genetic mechanisms by which embryos establish early polarity vary dramatically from one organism to the next.

The mechanisms by which embryos establish early polarity differ depending on whether the signals by which polarity is achieved are inscribed in the cytoplasm of the egg or the p-granules of the sperm.
Despite their apparent dissimilarity from species to species, the means by which organisms establish polarity rely on essentially the same genetic mechanisms.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
When we do an Author's *Opinion* question, we're often stopping to think whether the Author's voice was spread throughout the passage (giving us an Undefined Target) or whether it's fairly concentrated in one paragraph, typically the last one (giving us a Semi-Defined Target).

This passage seems to be the latter. The passage was mainly informative, but the last paragraph seemed to have more of the author's voice.

She sounded fascinated by a couple things:
- an *astonishing* conservation of mechanism in the processes that elaborate an organism's parts (the genes that build eyes, for example, are similar across many species)

- a *seeming* paradox that when organisms are at a uni-cellular or barely multi-cellular stage, they look the same but their developmental mechanisms are different. Later, the organisms look different but their developmental mechanisms are similar.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Pick any safely-worded answer we can support, but it's likely to relate to the author's thoughts in the final paragraph.

choices.text: The simpler the organism, the greater the speed at which it develops from fertilized egg to embryo.
choices.tag: Too Strong: more X, more Y
choices.explanation:
This *Volume Dial* formulation (the more X, the more Y) is the most extreme type of claim there is, because it extends infinitely in both directions.

A 20-celled organism's embryo develops faster than a 21-celled organism's embryo does.

An organism with 10 million cells develops faster than an organism with 11 million cells.

There's nothing in the passage that lets us say that for **all** life forms (that go from egg to embryo), the simpler it is, the faster it develops.

choices.text: Scientists have determined how polarity is established in most simple vertebrates.
choices.explanation:
The word "most" is one of the most frequent killers of answer choices in Reading Comp, Inference, and Necessary Assumption.

Do we really have this specificity anywhere in the passage?

We were told that scientists have figured out polarity for **at least 51%** of simple vertebrates?

The only time we hear about "simple vertebrates", in paragraph 2, we hear that:
*A similar sperm-driven mechanism is **thought** to establish body orientation in **some** comparatively simple vertebrates such as frogs*.

choices.text: Scientists will try to determine how polarity is established in humans.
choices.explanation:
This feels pretty strong on a first pass (scientists **will** try to determine?). It's pretty extreme to be so sure about the future.

However, the end of the 2nd paragraph does say that, "How polarity is established in mammals is currently **a tempting mystery** to researchers".

If an author thinks that X is a tempting mystery to researchers, then it's not a crazy rephrasing to think the author would agree that "some researchers will attempt to solve the mystery".

choices.text: Very few observations of embryonic development after polarity is established are generalizable to more than a single species.
choices.explanation:
The final paragraph is saying the opposite of this.

Very few observations of establishing polarity are generalizable. When it comes to the early stage of establishing polarity, species tend to vary widely.

Yet for the later stages of development, once polarity is established, there are sets of "essential genes that are remarkably similar among all life forms for elaboration of parts" (such as building a pair of eyes).

choices.text: Simpler organisms take longer to establish polarity than do more complex organisms.
choices.explanation:
The passage never makes any broad comparison between the length of time that simple organisms take to establish polarity vs. the length of time that more complex organisms do.

However, we have a simple organism like a fruit fly in which polarity is established before the egg is even fertilized, and we have more complex organisms like mammals in which many stages of cell division transpire before polarity is established.

So from the tiny examples we do know, this comparison is backwards.

questions.prompt: The passage provides information to suggest that which one of the following relationships exists between the development of humans and the development of fruit flies?

choices.text: Since humans and fruit flies use similar genetic material in their development, analogies from fruit fly behavior can be useful in explaining human behavior.
For the elaboration of parts, human development relies on genetic material quite different in nature, though not in quantity, from that of a fruit fly.
Positional information for establishing polarity in a human embryo, as in that of the fruit fly, is distributed throughout the egg prior to fertilization.

A study of the development of the fruit fly’s visual system would more likely be applicable to questions of human development than would a study of the mechanisms that establish the fruit fly’s polarity.
While the fruit fly egg becomes a larva in a single day, a human embryo takes significantly longer to develop because humans cannot develop limbs until they have established a nervous system.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, polarity is established in a human embryo

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Towards the end of the 2nd paragraph it says that,

*Research indicates that in **human** and other mammalian **embryos**, polarity develops much later (than when the sperm first fertilizes the egg), as many stages of cell division occur with no apparent asymmetries among cells.*

We don't know how polarity *does* occur, but we know it's not inscribed in the egg and it's not triggered by sperm fertilizing the egg. It happens later in the developmental process.

choices.text: after more stages of cell division than in frogs
choices.explanation:
The end of the 2nd paragraph tells us that "a similar sperm-drive mechanism is thought to establish polarity in frogs". And the following sentence says "research indicates that in human embryos, polarity develops much later, as many stages of cell division occur with no apparent asymmetries among cells".

Putting those two consecutive thoughts together, we know that human polarity is established after more stages of cell division than for frog polarity.

choices.text: before the sperm enters the egg
choices.explanation: We know that fruit flies have early polarity established (before sperm even enters egg). Frogs have polarity established later (when sperm enters egg). Humans have polarity established later than that (after sperm has entered the egg and many stages of cell division have occurred).

choices.text: after positional information is provided by the massing of p-granules
choices.explanation:
Scientists don't know **how** humans establish polarity, so we can't say anything about whether p-granules are involved.

We only know **when** humans establish polarity, in a very fuzzy way: *after many stages of cell division have already occurred*.

choices.text: by the same sperm-driven mechanism as in the nematode
choices.explanation:
Scientists don't know **how** humans establish polarity, so we can't say anything about whether a sperm-driven mechanism is involved.

We only know **when** humans establish polarity, in a very fuzzy way: *after many stages of cell division have already occurred*.

The sperm-driven mechanism of the nematode means that polarity is established in that very first cell, before any cell division has occurred, so there probably isn't any way it could be true that humans have the same sperm-driven mechanism.

choices.text: in the same way as in simpler vertebrates
choices.explanation:
We're told that, "a similar sperm-driven mechanism is thought to establish polarity in some comparatively simple vertebrates such as frogs, though **apparently not** in more complex vertebrates such as mammals."

Since humans are mammals, the passage is telling us that polarity is **not** achieved in the same way as in simpler vertebrates.

questions.prompt: By " conservation of mechanism " (second sentence of the last paragraph) the author is probably referring to

choices.text: how the same mechanism can be used to form different parts of the same organism
the fact that no genetic material is wasted in development
how few genes a given organism requires in order to elaborate its parts
a highly complex organism’s requiring no more genetic material than a simpler one
the fact that analogous structures in different species are brought about by similar genetic means

to elaborate on the differences between embryonic formation in the fruit fly and in the nematode
to suggest why the process of establishing early polarity in humans is not yet understood

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is a major difference between the establishment of polarity in the fruit fly and in the nematode?

choices.text: The fruit fly embryo takes longer to establish polarity than does the nematode embryo.
The mechanisms that establish polarity are more easily identifiable in the nematode than in the fruit fly.
Polarity signals for the fruit fly embryo are inscribed entirely in the egg and these signals for the nematode embryo are inscribed entirely in the sperm.

questions.prompt: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
On Primary Purpose, we try to prephrase based on language from our Framework.

We would have probably called this passage a *Highlight Noteworthy* passage centered around the topic of establishing polarity in an embryo.

Why did the author find this topic noteworthy? What's special / interesting / important about embryo polarity?

The author seems most fascinated by the paradox described in the last paragraph: even though there's tons of **variety** in terms of how each species establishes polarity within an embryo (much of it unknown), *after* the organism has established polarity, there's tons of **similarity** in terms of how the new stages of development go.

choices.text: articulate a theory of how early polarity is established and support the theory by an analysis of data
choices.tag: Out of Scope: articulate a theory
choices.explanation: There's no unitary theory of how early polarity is established. The passage is emphasizing that there are lots of different ways that early polarity is established.

choices.text: describe a phase in the development of organisms in which the genetic mechanisms used are disparate and discuss why this disparity is surprising
choices.explanation:
"Establishing polarity" is a phase in the development of organisms, so, yes, the passage describes the phase where organisms establish polarity.

Does the passage say that the genetic mechanisms are disparate?

Yes, this is half of the paradox we were looking for. As the final paragraph says, "the mechanisms of development used [to establish polarity] are vastly different".

Does the author discuss why this disparity is surprising?

Yes, she calls it a "seeming paradox". Paradoxes are inherently surprising. It's surprising that organisms vary so much in terms of how they establish polarity, because once they've established polarity, "there is an **astonishing** conservation of mechanism --- the developmental mechanisms used are remarkably similar" when it comes to building eyes and ears and spinal cords and such.

choices.text: provide a classification of the mechanisms by which different life forms establish early polarity
choices.explanation:
The author definitely discusses several mechanisms by which different life forms establish early polarity.

But does she provide a *classification*?

Does she say, "birds use p-granules, amphibians use a pre-polarized egg, mammals use X, etc.?"

No, there are just a handful of one-off examples. We know how the fruit fly establishes polarity and how *certain* nematodes establish polarity. She then says that some simple vertebrates might do something similar, but no one really knows what more complex vertebrates like mammals do.

So it's hard to say that there's any classification system provided. This answer also would do a worse job than the correct answer does of describing what happens in the final paragraph.

choices.text: argue that a certain genetic process must occur in all life forms, regardless of their apparent dissimilarity
choices.tag: Too Strong: must occur in all
choices.explanation:
The author never says anything super-extreme like "there is a genetic process that must occur in all life forms".

We could potentially say that the first sentence identifies "establishing polarity" as something that must occur in all life forms for an embryo to develop". But the author isn't *arguing* that must occur. She just states that it does occur and then starts talking about different ways that it occurs.

choices.text: explain why an embryo must establish early polarity before it can develop into an organism
choices.explanation:
The author never explains why an embryo must establish early polarity. It's just sort of common sense that you can't build a building if you don't know which direction is up and which direction is down.

Similarly, DNA can't build an organism if it doesn't have an initial sense of top vs. bottom. The author never explains this, and it's certainly not what the bulk of the passage is doing.
